author: Majid Maleki Meighani
title: The Radicalism of Form and the Radicalism of Content
content:
The wave of high-school protests in France, which began in late September 2026 in the suburbs of Paris and spread to many other cities, has revived an old question on the radical left: is a riot left-wing simply because its form is radical? Drawing on the Marxist tradition, this article separates three levels of analysis: the social cause of a protest, the form the struggle takes, and its political direction. It argues that these do not necessarily coincide. The legitimacy of a demand does not guarantee the legitimacy of every form of action. The radicalism of a form of struggle does not guarantee the radicalism of its political content. And the political outcome of a movement is not necessarily what its first participants intended. The left’s criterion should be neither the intensity of images from the street nor even the form of action itself, but the capacity to convert scattered anger into organized social power. The article warns against two traps at once: glorifying disorder for its own sake, and accepting the frame in which the state reduces every protest to “urban violence.”

The current protests in France began with entirely material grievances: a shortage of teachers, overcrowded classrooms, decaying school buildings, mounting pressure to perform, and anxiety about a future that looks less secure to much of this generation than it did to the last. The first protests t

author: Tahrir Hamdi
title: Palestine Resists: From Fanon and Kanafani to Armed Struggle and Return
content:
How does one resist dispossession and displacement, ongoing genocide, culturicide, scholasticide and epistemicide, and all forms of erasure of a people’s past, present and future? The answer: Resist by all available means—armed resistance, cultural resistance, and economic resistance; this is a legal right recognized under international law, but before that, it is morally legitimate, justified, and necessary. Israel is a brutal settler colony that was made possible by two main strategies: the expulsion of the Palestinian people from their indigenous land (historic Palestine) and ongoing genocide that is now 78 years old.

Armed resistance, as theorized by anti-colonial theorists such as Frantz Fanon, Aimé Césaire, Amílcar Cabral, Ghassan Kanafani, and Edward Said, is an essential part of the anti-colonial struggle for the liberation of colonized minds and lands. In his book The Wretched of the Earth (1963), Frantz Fanon, a psychiatrist by training, forcefully argued for anti-colonial armed resistance, stating precisely because colonization is such a violent and dehumanizing process, “decolonization is always a violent phenomenon” (35). For Fanon, colonization always dehumanizes the colonized; therefore, the colonized must use violence against the colonizer to allow for the rehumanization of the colonized because revolutionary violence is meant to end the oppression, colonizatio

author: Binoy Kampmark
title: Sportswashing the Racing Circuit: Rwanda and Formula One
content:
Tyrants and demagogues love sports and the governing bodies that preside over them. Despite strictures, injunctions and warnings about dealing with unsavoury regimes, a sporting body or organisation can always be relied on to ignore the fine print of their charters and make a dash for the revenue till. While the candidates for such a list are long – the International Olympic Committee and the world footballing body FIFA figure with amoral sprightliness in that regard – Formula One (F1) has shown itself to be most promiscuous.

In its October 13 statement, FI glows with the announcement that motor racing will “return to Africa for the first time since 1993.” Then, the apartheid government of South Africa, one nearing expiration, still offered their good services to F1 to run the tournament as part of a controversial tradition. (The South African Grand Prix had been something of a fixture since the 1960s, barring the interrupting hiccup in the latter 1980s.) In a ten-year agreement with the Rwandan government, the Formula 1 African Grand Prix will become a part of the racing calendar in the early 2030s, beginning its first race at the still to be completed Bugesera circuit. “The new track will be developed to FIA Grade 1 standards as part of a wider sports, tourism, infrastructure, and commercial development project led by the Rwanda Development Board.”

author: Ramzy Baroud
title: What Does the Green Party’s Historic Anti-Zionist Motion Mean for Palestine?
content:
The Green Party has put the conversation back on track: the problem is not the lack of creative solutions to the Israeli occupation of Palestine. The problem is Zionism itself.

To appreciate the significance of Motion A105, adopted by the Green Party of England and Wales on October 4, consider its basic tenets.

The party is now formally anti-Zionist. It endorses the Palestinian right of return, supports one democratic state throughout historic Palestine, reaffirms its commitment to the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement, distinguishes anti-Zionism from antisemitism, and calls for a full arms embargo against Israel.

Though the decision may seem revolutionary within British politics, it is hardly revolutionary when examined against the history of Palestinian dispossession, beginning long before the Nakba of 1948.

Indeed, the Greens were not the first to equate Zionism with racism. That history owes much to Africa’s anti-colonial movements and their struggle against apartheid.

In 1975, the Organization of African Unity, meeting in Kampala, Uganda, drew explicit parallels between the racial systems governing South Africa, Rhodesia and occupied Palestine, identifying their common imperialist origins.

This position helped lay the groundwork for UN General Assembly Resolution 3379, adopted on November 10, 1975, which determined that Zionism was a form of racism and

author: Hamilton Nolan
title: We Infiltrated a Police Union Convention in Las Vegas
content:
The gruff man at the microphone on the stage in the front of the meeting room in the Paris casino in Las Vegas was complaining about Las Vegas. How it’s hot. How it’s expensive. And how, having come here hoping for a thriving and successful convention, his organization now found itself thwarted by a straitjacket of absurd institutional rules.

“You can’t even move a box from left to right without contacting someone to do that,” he grumbled.

Could you blame him for being peevish? There were only about 50 people in the room. Not really an attendance to brag about. It was 109 degrees outside on this late August day. The big water bottles in the rooms’ minibars went for $15 each. And these convention contracts with big Vegas resorts did, in fact, come with lots of rules—no doubt due to the fact that every single property on the Vegas strip is fully unionized. These unions, with their crazy regulations and sky high prices! It was enough to drive any convention planner mad.

The weird thing was: we were at a union convention.

Technically, at least. This was the 23rd Annual Convention of the International Union of Police Associations (IUPA), which represents tens of thousands of cops in local departments from coast to coast. Though not the largest police union in America, IUPA has the distinction of being the only police union that is a member of the AFL-CIO. It joined the labor fed

author: Daniel Gauss
title: The 50th Anniversary of the Thammasat University Massacre (1976, Bangkok): Why It Still Matters
content:
Thammasat in the Context of Student Protests around the World

Why, in the late 1960s, did university student protests begin in differing parts of the world, in widely varying societies? Postwar governments had greatly expanded higher education to supply the skilled professionals needed by growing economies and to make social mobility/meritocracy more possible. This brought unprecedented numbers of largely middle-class students into universities, creating concentrated communities with the intelligence, formal education, time and organizational networks to engage in politics.

These students then encountered hypocritical contradictions between the ideals they were taught and the societies around them. Governments were defending freedom while fighting colonial wars, democracies tolerated and supported racial inequality, economic inequality and class struggle became more apparent and universities themselves helped to reproduce social inequality through their class and race-based admissions processes.

Learning about Vietnam, decolonization, civil-rights struggles and economic injustice transformed universities into hotbeds of radicalized students who had no trouble questioning and opposing what had been blithely accepted in the past.

Thammasat University in Bangkok can be understood within this context. Indeed, I am writing this essay because Thammasat remains one of the most ove

author: Marcos Rupérez Cerqueda
title: ‘Inner Degrowth’: An Engineer on Why the Energy Crisis and Our Inner Emptiness are the Same Problem
content:
Marcos Rupérez Cerqueda spent years as an engineer on green hydrogen projects in Spain, installing electrolysers and fuel cells, before the numbers made him stop believing in a technical fix. His new book, Inner Degrowth: From Energy Collapse to Existential Void, with a foreword by the Spanish physicist Antonio Turiel, follows that path from the energy data to a much more personal question. In this Q&A, he traces this journey and discusses his upcoming book.

I grew up inside the solution. My father is an engineer who chaired an environmental foundation, and we lived in one of the first bioclimatic houses in my region of Spain. So when I chose what to study, it felt obvious: industrial engineering, then a master’s in hydrogen in Denmark. If most of the energy that moves our civilization isn’t electricity, hydrogen looked like the perfect bridge: make it with renewables, store it, move it, use it.

Then one afternoon, in front of a spreadsheet with my business partner, I did the full count for one common chain. Around 40% of the energy is lost in the electrolyser, roughly another 10% compressing the hydrogen, and another 40 to 50% turning it back into electricity in a fuel cell. Of every 100 units of renewable electricity you put in, only 20 to 25 come out at the end. That isn’t a problem better engineering can fix. It’s thermodynamics. author: Javier Moreno Zacarés
title: Fifteen Years Later
content:
Fifteen years after the indignados occupied the Puerta del Sol, Madrid’s central plaza is once again the locus of a mass movement that has brought Spain to a political impasse. How are we back here again? The immediate trigger was the eviction of an elderly tenant. Maricarmen Abascal, who had occupied her rent-capped apartment in central Madrid since 1956, was expelled from her home on 23 September after the investment fund Urbagestión acquired the property and exploited a legal loophole to quintuple her rent. Maricarmen’s age and vulnerability – the 87-year-old was removed on a hospital bed and has since died – made it a particularly egregious breach of the moral economy. The case struck a nerve, prompting a political storm; the government has now announced a snap election. As protests spread nationwide, the encampment at Puerta del Sol consolidated under the leadership of the Sindicato de Inquilinas, Madrid’s tenant union. Media outlets are reporting on the motions passed at the open-air general assembly. One decision has been of particular public interest: a general strike for the right to housing, announced for 11 November, a few weeks before the election.

author: Ruhi Bhasin
title: How Gen Z Protests Are Reshaping Politics in Asia
content:
Asia has seen a surge of “Gen Z protests,” led by a generation tired of accepting the status quo and increasingly using social media to drive change in deeply entrenched political systems. In India, protests over the education system helped force the education minister’s resignation in 2026. Protests in Bangladesh and Nepal in 2024 and 2025, respectively, led to government changes. These protests have helped expose fractured political structures in these countries.

Governments in several South and Southeast Asian countries have done little to address the economic distress and corruption plaguing them. The Gen Z citizens, who are facing the brunt of these crumbling systems, are increasingly demanding accountability and justice, using social media to fight back, organize, document events, and press their demands. Despite efforts to suppress them, these protests have brought political change. Whether these movements can sustain solidarity and organize beyond immediate demands to pursue lasting reforms remains to be seen.

In India, the Bharatiya Janata Party-led government has been in power for more than 12 years, having first been elected in 2014. Press freedom and other democratic safeguards have come under pressure during its tenure; Sweden’s V-Dem Institute has classified India as an “electoral autocracy.” As stated by an August 2026 Time report, “Modi has consolidated his gr

author: Patrick Bond
title: Navi Pillay’s Nobel Peace Prize Spotlights South African and Global Battles for Justice
content:
Judge Navi Pillay’s Nobel Peace Prize award on October 9 was a rare bit of very good news. “If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump,” she said, laughing, alongside Nuremberg Forum members in Germany, upon hearing the news. She was attending a commemoration of the Nazi war-crimes prosecution that ended in October 1946. Pillay’s willingness to attack broader socio-political conditions reflects a long history of fusing ideological radicalization and practical reforms.

Yet at the very same time, a xenophobic movement – ‘March and March’ – was rioting and burning cars both in Pillay’s native Durban and in Johannesburg next to South Africa’s Constitutional Court. The vigilantes were both trying to influence the November 4 municipal elections (and will do so again and again in the next few weeks), and specifically protesting the state’s new implementation of a ConCourt ruling that empowered immigrants through a more generous interpretation of asylum regulations.

And the same day, their own Zulu nationalist leader, 84-year old Jacob Zuma – who was SA President from 2009-18 – was reported to be on his last legs at a KwaZulu-Natal hospital. If he passes on, that could inflame matters further this week, requiring a more extensive army deployment to the province.

author: M. Reza Behnam
title: The Imperial Pen: Geopolitical Vandalism in West Asia
content:
For centuries, the lands stretching from the Levant to the Persian Gulf have been subjected to a strange form of conceptual alchemy. Driven by Western Orientalist scholarship, colonial cartography and modern geopolitical agendas, the dynamic, pluralistic mosaic of West Asia has been systematically reduced to a monolithic caricature, defined by violence, archaic fundamentalism, and in need of rescue.

These mutations are more than mere scholarly failures; they represent a destructive erasure of history. By denying complex societies their natural path toward modernity and stripping them of historical agency, these misrepresentations serve to validate existing systems of oppression.

To truly understand contemporary Arab West Asia, one must recognize that its political boundaries and power dynamics are essentially an imperialist artifact; and that it remains shackled to a modern version of the colonial 1916 Sykes-Picot ghost: artificial borders drawn by foreign pens, hyper-economies addicted to petrodollars, governance models built and local rulers chosen to appease external patrons and crush internal dissent.

British and French colonialists, Mark Sykes and Francois Georges Picot, engineered the systemic underdevelopment of West Asia, through calculated geopolitical vandalism. By secretly carving up Ottoman lands into European spheres of influence during World War I, with total d

author: JoEllen Chernow
title: What If We Organized Survivors of Sexual Violence?
content:
Every few months America discovers another “monster.” A celebrity. A billionaire. A politician. A religious leader. A professor. A CEO.

The details differ, but the story doesn’t: rape survivors risk everything revealing years of abuse, followed by a burst of public outrage and demands for accountability.

Survivors of Jeffrey Epstein told us about a global rape and sex-trafficking network in which young people were abused and exploited by some of the world’s wealthiest and most influential men. For decades, survivors were ignored, disbelieved, and failed by the institutions around them. Newly released files corroborating their horror stories have resulted in zero US criminal arrests and little tangible accountability.

The #MeToo movement was supposed to interrupt this cycle. For a brief moment in 2017, it seemed possible that we could stop treating each “scandal” as an isolated incident and confront the systems connecting them. Instead, less than three months after the hashtag went viral, the press was full of opinion pieces about how it had all “gone too far.” The backlash flipped #MeToo into #NotAllMen. Outrage faded into fatalism, denial, and eventually business as usual.

As a rape survivor, community activist, and labor organizer, I call bullshit.

The problem isn’t that we keep “discovering” abusive men. It’s that we keep refusing to look at the underlying systems that

author: Roxanne D. Brown
title: The Inspiration That Leads Workers to Unionize
content:
Davion Johnson long realized that they and their colleagues deserved higher pay, fairer treatment, and greater respect at the Corning plant in Hemlock, Michigan.

But nothing drove home the need for change more than a supervisor’s callous response when a coworker fell from a ladder.

Instead of calling an ambulance, Johnson recalled, the supervisor threatened to dock the injured man a sick day if he left to seek care on his own.

An angry Johnson subsequently helped to lead 1,400 coworkers in a successful union drive with the United Steelworkers (USW). Now, they wield a collective voice on safety, pay, and other issues as they do the important work of manufacturing components for the nation’s solar industry.

Rampant inequality continues to fuel record support for unions nationwide. In all, 71 percent of Americans now approve of unions, and a growing number want organized labor to have more influence in American life, a new Gallup poll found.

Johnson’s experience shows why.

With costs of groceries, healthcare, utilities, and mortgages all skyrocketing, everyday families are falling further behind in today’s economy than they did during the pandemic.

Banding together empowers workers to fight for the higher wages they need to survive an affordability crisis that’s battering everyone except the uberwealthy. Studies show that union workers make higher wages, on average, than no

author: Steve Ellner
title: Delcy Rodríguez is Bending Over Backward to Accommodate Washington
content:
Venezuelan provisional president Delcy Rodríguez’s all-smiles photo op with Trump in a Manhattan hotel on September 22 proved too much for some of her erstwhile supporters. For the Spanish leftist Juan Carlos Monedero, a staunch defender of Hugo Chávez, Maduro and at first Rodríguez, her New York appearance “clashed with the previous socialist and anti-imperialist discourse” of her movement.

Shortly before the encounter, Rodríguez evaded a reporter’s question about whether she would visit jailed Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro in Brooklyn. Her decision to stay clear of Maduro is consistent with her attempt to chart a new course for Venezuela.

Rodríguez became interim president following the bloody U.S. military incursion on January 3, 2026 that resulted in the kidnapping of Maduro and the First Lady Cilia Flores. Facing the prospect of a second, more devastating military attack, Rodríguez shifted sharply toward Washington on foreign and oil policy while reshuffling the public administration and military at the expense of hardline pro-Chávez (Chavista) loyalists.

Rodriguez’s strategy goes too far

author: Mohammed Altaj
title: Israel Above the Law … Palestine Beyond Justice
content:
The world did not lack knowledge of what was happening to Palestinians.

It knew that a people had been living under occupation for decades; that land was being confiscated, settlements expanding, homes demolished, and checkpoints cutting cities and villages off from one another.

The United Nations knew. Governments knew. Parliaments and international courts knew.

The shift now visible across significant parts of Western public opinion did not begin because the world suddenly discovered new facts about Palestine.

What changed was the distance between the news and the human being.

People saw what war means when a child is trapped beneath rubble, what displacement means when a family carries whatever it can and walks away without knowing where it will go.

And the numbers began to acquire names, faces and voices.

One of those names was Hind Rajab.

I do not mention Hind because her story encompasses everything that happened in Gaza. I mention her because some tragedies become windows through which people see what numbers alone cannot reveal.

Hind was trapped inside a car in Gaza in January 2024 after members of her family had been killed. She called for help. Twelve days later, she was found dead inside the car. The two paramedics sent to rescue her were also found dead.

But Hind was no longer a number.

author: Paul Buhle
title: The Communitarian Mind of Michael Albert
content:
Somewhere, in the complex and often confused history of anarchist and communitarian movements of the US, Michael Albert resides, now almost 80, a veteran of endless campaigns but still eager to make his familiar points. Communitarianism of some kind can work, can create a substitute for the miserable economic arrangements of the present, and engage ordinary people in the process of changing themselves as they endeavor to change the world.

This sentiment has a more than honorable history even in the US, historically known for its weak and fragile Left institutions. Its origins should properly be placed well before the rise of the Marxist-related movements, mostly German immigrants, during the 1860s-70s. Indeed, the communitarian experiments of the 1820s-40s engaged some of the great figures of the age, from Shakers to Bohemians, and even produced a remarkable literature, including Nathaniel Hawthorne’s rather satirical Blithedale Romance.

The ideas of dress reform (mainly for women), healthy foods, and even freer sexual relations flowed into Abolitionist and Women’s Rights movements. The Civil War swallowed a large chunk of utopianism, but enough survived to prompt a rebirth in successive generations. Edward Bellamy’s best-selling novel, Looking Backward , published in 1887, seemed, by example, to make small-scale cooperative living imaginable, even if colonies nearly always f

author: Mahdi Niksefat Motlagh
title: Ending the war requires accepting Iran in the Middle East
content:
The hardest question about ending the war with Iran belongs in Washington. What place can Iran occupy after the fighting stops? A country left economically excluded, unable to rebuild and exposed to renewed attack has little reason to regard a ceasefire as a durable ending. The war cannot be politically settled while Iranian recovery remains an unacceptable outcome.

The latest diplomacy leaves that question unresolved. Tehran has received US feedback, through Qatar, on a seven-day trust-building proposal. Yet on 1 October, the US Treasury expanded sanctions against Iran’s automotive and rail sectors, alongside manufacturing and steel networks. Talks about ending the confrontation are proceeding alongside measures that further restrict Iran’s capacity to sustain its economy.

The Islamic Republic connects these claims to a revolutionary and religious account of its purpose. Ali Khamenei’s 2019 Second Phase statement, with its emphasis on building an Islamic civilisation, expressed that connection explicitly. Security, within this understanding, includes the capacity to continue a political project.

author: Abe Walker
title: The Battle for the Soul of the UAW: Union Democracy and the Seductions of Power
content:
After years of struggling in relative obscurity, democratic socialists were jubilant to have elected one of their own to high-profile office. With bold rhetoric and meme-friendly soundbites, their candidate captured the hearts and minds of a working-class base eager for an alternative to the establishment’s caustic brand of demagoguery. Ignoring calls for moderation, the campaign took on a defiant, openly confrontational tone. Its outcome shocked the old guard, upended the status quo, and served as a warning to entrenched interests everywhere.

The year was 2023, and Shawn Fain had just won the presidency of the United Auto Workers union. Fain quickly became the public face of a resurgent workers movement that seemed poised to usher in a new wave of labor militancy. But there would be little time for celebration once the weight of the task ahead set in. Indeed – like a certain big city mayor – Fain would quickly discover that his election fight was only a preview of the battles to come.

Fain is now standing for reelection, with ballots set to be tallied next month. Three years ago, few could imagine that Fain would face a viable challenger as he eyed a second term. Yet today, his star has long since dimmed, and his fate now hangs in balance. The upcoming vote will serve as a referendum on his tenure, and while he remains the clear favorite, there is considerably less enthusias

author: Patrick Egan
title: White Nationalism’s Appeal Runs Deeper Than Partisan Politics
content:
As Americans prepared to celebrate the nation’s 250th birthday on the morning of July 4, sobering images flashed across their phones and TV screens. Hundreds of masked men marched the streets of Washington carrying flags and chanting “Reclaim America!” It soon became clear from the logos on their identical baseball caps that the marchers were members of Patriot Front, a white nationalist group.

The march ended without incident. Still, it joined the 2017 “Unite the Right” rally in Charlottesville, Virginia, and the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol – both of which culminated in deadly violence – as recent mass demonstrations with participants who openly embrace white nationalism. Members of a loosely organized movement that usually operates out of public view, white nationalists hold that shifting demographics pose an existential threat to the white race, which they view as culturally superior and deserving of power over other groups in the U.S.

Combined with the spread of white nationalist ideology from obscure corners of the internet into mainstream politics, these events have led many Americans to wonder: How extensive is white nationalism’s appeal among the broader public, and who is drawn to this extremist ideology?

author: Branko Marcetic
title: According to Polls, Americans Like Socialism a Lot
content:
A crop of recent polls shows that socialism’s appeal is surprisingly broad. They also reflect a transformed US political landscape that is ripe for a socialist politician to capitalize on — if they’re willing to step up.

Socialism is more popular than it’s been for a long time, both socialism and its most well-known adherents appeal to a surprisingly diverse voter base, and most people still have no idea who Hasan Piker is.

Those are just a few of the takeaways from a crop of polls conducted over the past month or so, which together suggest the radicalized, antiestablishment zeal that’s taken over the Democratic electorate and opened the door for a rising socialist insurgency is still going strong, with a few surprises in tow. And they come at a potentially crucial time, as socialist Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez weighs whether to make a run for president in 2028, a campaign that many socialists view as pivotal to the future prospects of their movement as a whole.

We should obviously be careful with polls, which are not actual elections and only give us an imperfect snapshot of public opinion at any point in time. Still, while they may not exactly reflect hard numbers, they do often reflect real trends, especially when put alongside other poll results. And as such, these recent ones offer several takeaways.

author: D K Renton
title: Forgiveness is Part of Socialism
content:
When I tell people I’m interested in the politics of forgiveness, that often surprises them: the idea sounds bad and moralistic. I invite them to consider that the whole point of a revolution is to start over. The people who will change the world must start in this one — a system that rewards selfishness and cruelty. Accepting people despite their past harms is a fundamental part of building a new society.

Some socialists say that the left doesn’t need ethics. Marx and Engels wrote that Communism would end morality: ‘Communism abolishes eternal truths, it abolishes all religion, and all morality.’ But Marx also said that if Communism won, life would follow different rules: ‘From each according to his ability, to each according to his needs.’ What’s that, if not a description of a better society? In The German Ideology, Marx says this about revolutions: in them, we rid ourselves of ‘all the muck of ages and become fitted to found society anew.’ People change; without that possibility, you couldn’t have socialism.

When writing about forgiveness, there are three big ideas that matter most to me. First, forgiveness is an act done by victims — not their friends, and definitely not the state. The victim must achieve justice. Afterwards, you ask them if they want to forgive: in a situation of ongoing harm, asking a victim isn’t an act of generosity; it’s cruel.

author: Progressive International
title: From Law to Justice
content:
As Trump attacked the ICC and Netanyahu faced a walkout at the UN, forty states gathered to put an arms embargo, protections for the Court and a new UN mechanism modelled on the Special Committee against Apartheid.

Last week, the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) counted what remained of Gaza’s economy after almost three years of genocide and almost two decades of siege. Ninety-two per cent of its economic establishments have been damaged or destroyed. Unemployment has reached 78 per cent. GDP per person fell to $212 last year — barely 17 per cent of its pre-genocide level — while less than 1.5 per cent of Gaza’s cropland remains accessible and undamaged. Recovery and reconstruction will cost at least $71.5 billion. Pedro Manuel Moreno, acting head of UNCTAD, called it “the world’s most severe economic crisis on record”.

These were the conditions in which the governments of the world assembled in New York for the 81st United Nations General Assembly. On Monday 21 September, a thousand gathered at Riverside Church to celebrate the Charter on which the institution was founded, hosted by South Africa. Martin Luther King Jr stood in the same church in 1967 to deliver Beyond Vietnam. author: Céli Pinto
title: The Most Important Election in Brazilian History
content:
We usually say that in general elections, we’re choosing a president, governors and lawmakers for the next four years. That much seems obvious. But in this election, with the first round on October 4 and the runoff on October 25, we’re not just choosing who governs. We’re choosing the country’s future for decades to come.

This isn’t a choice between candidate A and candidate B. It’s a choice between a sharp lurch toward colonized totalitarianism and the survival of democracy. Every voter needs to have this clearly in mind. We are responsible for this country’s future. Future generations will blame us, and rightly so, if we fail and Brazil is handed over to colonizer vultures.

Voters, whether or not they are politically active, whether they are young, middle-aged or elderly, have plenty of issues with the current government. It’s true the government could have done more, particularly if it didn’t have a Congress dedicated almost exclusively to serving its own interests. Even so, the government accomplished a great deal. It did this not despite Congress, but because Congress exists. That made it possible to negotiate with lawmakers and to pressure them through the press and social media.

author: Binoy Kampmark
title: Denial as a Way of Life: Netanyahu on Egyptian Warnings About October 7
content:
Things are looking bleaker by the day for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, most notably for his standing as a competent leader in full mastery of his office. After allegations were made that he had received warnings from the United Arab Emirates leader President Mohamed bin Zayed (MBZ) that the October 7, 2023 attack by Hamas was, if not imminent then certainly most likely, a sense of paralytic denial has taken hold.

The claim by Haaretz, based on research for the book Hostages: 843 Days of Abandonment by Shlomi Eldar and Ruth Yuval, finds Netanyahu being told, in unambiguous terms, that an attack by Hamas was being planned. A 45-minute conversation apparently took place between the UAE President and Netanyahu, in which the Emirati leader warned of the potentially destabilising intentions of the late Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar. Talks between Hamas and Netanyahu’s office that had begun in 2023 in search of temporary truce had stalled. Sinwar was getting testy.

The Egyptian intelligence chief Abbas Kamel has also emerged as another prominent figure to bulk the warnings on Hamas’s ominous intentions, with The Wall Street Journal reporting as much on September 27. author: Thomas Klikauer
title: German Natural Gas Politics – Profits or Ingenuity
content:
According to the IEA‘s global electricity mix, non-renewable, unsustainable and highly polluting fossil fuels still make up 57% of electricity production with the much talked about oil – Strait of Hormuz, etc. – being just 2%. Oil is used to make petrol for cars still running on combustion engines, but it is not much used to make electricity.

By contrast, renewables come in at an ever-increasing percentage with wind and solar are 17% and hydropower 14%. Not to be forgotten: the atomic power of Chernobyl and Fukushima, at 9%.

In Germany, solar makes up 33%, coal 27%, natural gas 13%, wind 11%, biomass 9% and others 7%. According to Germany’s “windmesse.de”, Germany runs on 62% renewable energy for electricity generation. Sadly, natural gas still made up 13.4%.

Worldwide, the share of natural gas in global electricity generation fell from 23.9% in 2020 to 21.8% in 2025. Still, gas remains the world’s second-largest source of electricity generation with a 22% share of total output, behind only coal at 33%. Gas makes up a much bigger slice in places like the US (40%) than in, for example, India (2%) or China (3%).

Despite all this, Germany is at a critical point in its energy transition towards renewables. While Germany’s conservative government fancies building new gas-fired power plants, this raises a fundamental question: is Germany building a bridge to a carbon-neutral age?

author: Abba Solomon
title: When Law Fails: A Jew Reads Confronting Zionism
content:
I am, maybe, a reader at cross-purposes from this book’s intent. I translate the challenge of fighting Zionist oppression of Palestine gentiles, somewhat automatically, also to the question, How do we redeem Jewish identity?

Confronting Zionism, by international law scholars Noura Erakat and John Reynolds, reviews the colonial and imperialist legal assumptions in the Balfour declaration, the League of Nations Mandate, and the May 1948 declaration of the State of Israel.

Once seen, it is hard to unsee, the principles that Erakat and Reynolds name as the face of Zionism to Palestinians: domination and dehumanization.

Their work is about failed attempts to use international institutions to protect Gaza since October 7, 2023, and during Zionism’s stages for the past 100 years in its accomplishment of Jewish nationalist rule of Palestine. They analyze the colonial assumptions in international structures that made the conquest feasible.

There’s a lot of cognitive dissonance in being a Jew reading a recounting of Zionist torment of Palestine – reconciling lifetime programming of being of a special and persecuted people, with industrial-scale targeting of non-Jews because they live where nationalist Jews covet.
